prompt.context:
Apartment Co is a residential real estate company that owns and operates 10 buildings throughout three different boroughs within New York. The buildings were built between 1975 and 1990 and have been under Apartment Co.'s management since that time. Apartment Co. prides itself on offering affordable, quality apartments for everyday New Yorkers. The only permanent staff in Apartment Co.'s buildings are the doormen. The company operates leasing from their central location in Manhattan, and has contracted with a maintenance service, which will be up for renegotiation soon.

Over the last three years, Apartment Co has decided to invest $5M in its infrastructure with the hope of commanding higher apartment rent prices. The company has upgraded many of its apartment unit amenities, including kitchen appliances, bathroom fixtures, and flooring. These improvements have yielded high renter demand as well as increased rent prices. Recently, half of Apartment Co.'s buildings added washers and dryers in the basement; the remaining buildings have no laundry facilities. Even in light of these changes, however, management has not seen the increase in profitability it was hoping for. Apartment Co has asked your team to assess ways to achieve higher long-term profitability.
prompt.question: Apartment Co. has not seen the increase in profitability it was hoping for despite significant infrastructure investments. Assess ways to achieve higher long-term profitability.

clarifying_info.q: What are the company's revenue sources?
clarifying_info.a: The company's sole revenue source is tenant rent; other sources like vending machines and laundry machines are negligible.

clarifying_info.q: How many units are in each building?
How are the buildings distributed across boroughs?
clarifying_info.a: 5 buildings in Manhattan, 3 in Brooklyn, and 2 in Queens.

clarifying_info.q: Does the company own the buildings outright?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, all buildings under management are fully owned — no outstanding loans.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the maintenance/facilities staff?
clarifying_info.a: The company contracts a staff of 30 to maintain the apartment complexes.

clarifying_info.q: Has the real estate portfolio changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: No recent additions to their real estate portfolio.
Tenants are mostly young working professionals.

clarifying_info.q: Is the focus on immediate or long-term profitability?
clarifying_info.a: The focus is on long-term profitability; expenditures in the short-term must equate to a long-term profitability increase.

exhibits.title: Apartment Co. Financials
exhibits.shows: Three-year income summary (2016–2018) in $000s, showing revenue from tenant rent and a breakdown of costs including Property Management, Repair and Maintenance, Property Taxes, Occupancy (Utilities and Insurance), and Depreciation.

exhibits.title: Historic Electricity Rates ($/kWh)
exhibits.shows: Bar chart of electricity rates per kWh for each year from 2010 to 2018.

exhibits.title: Average Monthly Apartment Spend on Utilities
exhibits.shows: Stacked or grouped bar chart showing average monthly spend per apartment on Gas and Water for 2016, 2017, and 2018, with the y-axis ranging from $0 to $60.
exhibits.data: Gas and Water components shown per year 2016–2018; exact per-unit values readable from chart (approximate total ~$50–$60/month/unit in 2018).

exhibits.title: Real Estate Management Salaries (2017)
exhibits.shows: Chart comparing average management salary and average annual raise by years of experience (2, 5, 10, 20, 30+ years). Note indicates the average salary for Apartment Co. Management is $67K/year.

exhibits.title: Income Level of Residents
exhibits.shows: Pie chart breaking down the income distribution of current residents across five income brackets.

framework: Revenue: Analyze occupancy rates, current vs. market rent prices, and annual rent increase rates across Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens buildings
Variable Costs: Utilities (electricity, gas, water — note company began covering utilities in 2017), amenities upkeep, hourly/contract labor, maintenance contract (up for renegotiation)
Fixed Costs: Property management team salaries, insurance, property taxes, depreciation (spiked due to $5M infrastructure investment)
External Factors: Competing rent prices in the local market, borough-level demand trends, whether sector-wide profitability is declining

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what do the financials tell you about the profitability problem?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate will calculate profit for each year (Revenue minus Total Costs: 2016 = $7.7M, 2017 = $8.9M, 2018 = $8.9M in $000s) and identify that while revenue grew from $17M to $20.5M, total costs grew from $9.3M to $11.6M, squeezing margins. Key cost drivers to highlight: (1) Occupancy/Utilities jumped from $1.2M to $2.0M after management started paying utilities in 2017; (2) Depreciation jumped from $300K to $1M due to the $5M infrastructure investment. The candidate should zero in on utilities as the most actionable lever.

math.setup: Profit = Tenant Rent - Total Costs (all figures in $000s)
math.answer: Profit stabilized at ~$8.9M in 2017–2018 despite rising revenue; utilities and depreciation are the primary cost drivers eroding margin.

questions.prompt: Beginning in 2017, management decided to pay for utilities as part of the rental lease agreement to be competitive. What are some ways Apartment Co. can reduce their utilities expense?
questions.guidance: Good answers are bucketed into logical categories. Demand-side: encourage tenants to turn AC/lights off, incentive programs (reward for lowest energy consumption). Supply-side: building upgrades such as more efficient lighting (LED), solar paneling, automatic on/off sensors. Can also break down by utility type: electricity reduction strategies vs. gas vs. water. A great candidate offers creative ideas such as tenant energy-use competitions or gamified rewards.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the two most attractive electricity reduction strategies: installing energy-efficient LED lighting vs. installing solar panels. Which is the better investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should request installation cost, savings per unit, and lifespan for each option before calculating. They should compute total cost, annual savings, and breakeven period for each, then compare on NPV/payback logic. Solar panels have higher total savings over their lifespan; LED lighting has a faster payback period. A strong candidate notes that the company's strong cash position (no outstanding loans) may allow it to pursue both.

math.setup: LED Lighting: Cost = $30/bulb × (5,000 bulbs/bldg × 10 bldgs); Savings = kWh saved/bulb × total bulbs × $/kWh. Solar: Cost = $200/sq ft × 1,600 sq ft/bldg × 10 bldgs; Savings = kWh saved/sq ft × total sq ft × $/kWh.
steps: LED — Annual kWh saved: 100 kWh/bulb × 50,000 = 5,000,000 kWh
LED — Breakeven: $1,500,000 / $750,000 = 2 years; 8 years of net savings over 10-year lifespan
Solar — Total sq ft: 1,600 × 10 = 16,000 sq ft
Solar — Annual kWh saved: 400 kWh/sq ft × 16,000 = 6,400,000 kWh
Solar — Breakeven: $3,200,000 / $960,000 ≈ 3.3 years; ~17 years of net savings over 20-year lifespan
Solar total net savings over lifespan: $960,000 × 20 - $3,200,000 = $16,000,000
LED total net savings over lifespan: $750,000 × 10 - $1,500,000 = $6,000,000
math.answer: Solar panels: breakeven ~3 years, net savings ~$16M over 20 years. LED lighting: breakeven 2 years, net savings ~$6M over 10 years. Solar generates greater total savings; LED offers faster payback.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways that Apartment Co. can reduce their utilities expense?

categories.name: Demand-side (behavioral)
ideas: Encourage tenants to turn off AC when not home
Turn off lights when leaving rooms
Incentive/reward program for tenants with lowest monthly energy consumption

categories.name: Supply-side (infrastructure)
ideas: Install energy-efficient LED lighting throughout common areas and units

categories.name: Water reduction
ideas: Fix leaks proactively through maintenance contract renegotiation

categories.name: Gas reduction
ideas: Improve building insulation to reduce heating load
Programmable heating schedules for common areas

recommendation: Install solar panels: greatest annual savings ($960K/yr), highest total lifetime savings (~$16M), potential state/federal tax subsidies, 20-year lifespan with ~3-year breakeven
Alternatively, install LED lighting for a faster 2-year payback at lower upfront cost ($1.5M vs $3.2M) and ~$6M total savings
Best case: pursue both investments given no outstanding debt — the company can absorb the combined $4.7M upfront cost and capture $1.71M in combined annual savings
Renegotiate maintenance contract (coming up for renewal) to further reduce costs
Consider passing a portion of utility savings back as a competitive rent advantage to maintain occupancy
risks: Volatile energy prices: if electricity rates drop, savings projections fall short
High upfront capital costs for solar ($3.2M) may strain near-term liquidity
Tenants pilfering or damaging LED bulbs, increasing replacement costs
Opportunity cost: capital could be deployed into portfolio expansion or other renovations
Fickle consumer tastes may require further amenity investments to sustain rent levels
Solar: regulatory or permitting risk in NYC (roof access, zoning)
next_steps: Research and solicit bids from solar panel and LED lighting providers
Pilot the chosen solution in one building to validate savings projections before full rollout
Renegotiate the maintenance contract to secure cost reductions
Evaluate whether utility cost savings enable additional rent increases or justify further amenity upgrades
